The Shift

The demand is not local.

Two forces are converging in every dense city on earth at once. Commerce moved onto the phone, so goods now move in small parcels, fast, all day, on two wheels. And cities began pricing combustion out of their centers, starting with the districts where those deliveries are densest.

Vietnam is where those forces collide first and hardest, which is why we build here. It is not where the market ends. Jakarta, Manila, Bangkok, Delhi, Lagos, São Paulo: the same rider, the same parcel, the same math, a different flag.

01

E-commerce

Orders split into smaller, faster, more frequent drops. The parcel got lighter and the trip count exploded.

02

Urbanization

Denser cores, tighter streets, worse parking. Two wheels beat four on every metric that matters in a city center.

03

Regulation

The HCMC gasoline phase-out and Hanoi's low emission zone set a date. The transition is no longer optional or theoretical.

Who Rides

One bike, many working lives.

"Delivery rider" is not one job. In Vietnam alone the U-1 answers to a dozen different working days, and each one stresses the vehicle differently.

01

Food & Quick Commerce

Short hops, brutal frequency, two peaks a day. Insulated boxes up front, and swaps that fit inside a delivery window rather than breaking it.

02

Parcel & Last Mile

Volume over speed. Stacked cartons, long routes, and a payload rating that has to be real rather than optimistic.

03

Ride Hailing

Long hours, light loads, thin margins. Every đồng of running cost lands directly in the rider's own pocket.

04

Trade & Small Business

Market vendors, tradespeople and provincial shopkeepers moving their own stock. The bike is the delivery van they could never afford.

Move outward from Ho Chi Minh City and the pattern repeats with local accents: heavier loads and rougher roads in the provinces, tighter alleys in Hanoi's old quarter, longer distances across the Mekong Delta. Same platform, different rig.

Beyond The Shift

The same bike, off the clock.

A vehicle built to survive a working week is, by definition, built well enough for a weekend. The frame that carries 200 kg of parcels carries camping gear just as happily. The suspension tuned for broken city surfaces does not care that the broken surface is now a trail.

We did not design a second bike for this. Riders told us plainly that the machine they earn on is the machine they own, and it has to be worth riding when nobody is paying them. Adventure is not a different customer. It is the same customer on a Sunday.

Adventure configurations shown are design studies on the same U-1 chassis.

The Wider Map

Built in Vietnam. Not only for it.

We are deliberate about sequence. Vietnam first, because it is the hardest and most honest test bed on earth for a working electric two wheeler: extreme density, extreme duty cycles, unforgiving price sensitivity, and a regulatory clock already running.

A platform that earns its keep here does not need to be reinvented for Jakarta or Manila. The network agnostic battery bay is what makes that portable: every market has a different dominant swap operator, and a bike locked to one of them cannot cross a border. Ours can.

  1. Phase 01Vietnam

    Fleet first. Prove the platform under the hardest duty cycles and the tightest margins on earth.

  2. Phase 02Southeast Asia

    Jakarta, Manila, Bangkok. Density, climate and duty cycles closely match. Little needs to change.

  3. Phase 03Dense cities, anywhere

    Any market where commerce moved onto two wheels and the grid is catching up to it.
